chapter: Europe tours, Birdland memories and closing
title: Birdland engagements and the discovery of copied arrangements
summary: Cobb describes his graduated Birdland contract, then finds that George Rhodes and Reuben Phillips sold his scores to Willis Jackson, who played the same charts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I went to Birdland, and I had a graduated contract. I started with so much money a week, and each time I'd go back and get another $100.00 increase over a period of time. So I finally got in there now on one occasion. I'd played opposite many musicians, Dizzy Gillespie, (inaudible) Charlie Parker. I told you he used my rhythm section in there.

But I went in there one time with Willis Jackson, and George Rhodes was writing for me. Reuben Phillips was writing for me, and they keep the scores, and they was giving Willis same arrangement, and I'm trying to miss him, and he's trying to miss me without playing the same thing. I got so mad, boy, and George was with me on bass. I said, 'Man, you ought to be shame of yourself to make more money off the same arrangement you wrote for' -- I'm not lying to you.

And not -- we got to figure how we can miss one another and we won't get on the stand and play the same thing over. And they did that to me. And George did (inaudible) too. They kept the scores and just copied off for another band.
Well, that's very unusual, isn't it?
Well, they figured we'd never cross paths, but here we're working together, and when one come off, the other one goes on.
